body:
## Context

The Memory workspace has a 3D view of the memory graph (files, memory records, topics and their relations). It is one of SpaceApp's most visible features. Today it does not scale:

- **Rendering** (`apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/MemoryGraph3D.tsx`) uses Canvas 2D. Every frame it projects every node on the CPU, sorts all nodes by depth, strokes every edge as its own path and draws every node with `arc()`. Hover and click hit-testing is a linear scan.
- **Layout** (`layoutMemoryNetwork3D` in `memory-3d.ts`, run in `memory-network-layout.worker.ts`) is a fixed 180-step force simulation with a hash-map spatial grid that is rebuilt each step. It finishes before anything is drawn.
- **Data**: the overview endpoint (`GET /api/admin/memory/graph/overview` in `apps/api/src/memory-graph-routes.ts`) returns at most 2,000 nodes (`selectOverviewNodes`) and 6,000 edges. It sets `truncated: true` beyond that, so larger memories are only ever shown as a sample.

Long-running workspaces easily pass 2,000 nodes, and they are the users who get the most out of the memory graph.

## Goal

The 3D view renders and interacts smoothly with **50,000 nodes and 150,000 edges**, and lets the user load the full graph instead of a 2,000-node sample.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A WebGL2 renderer replaces the Canvas 2D drawing in the 3D view: instanced nodes, batched edges, depth handled by the GPU (no per-frame CPU sort of all nodes), and colors, sizes and focus/neighbor highlighting matching the current look.
- [ ] Picking (hover and click) takes at most 4 ms at 50k nodes, using GPU picking or a spatial index (no linear scan per pointer move).
- [ ] Labels: the current rules stay (core and source labels first, collision avoidance, the `showTitles` toggle), now with level-of-detail. At most a bounded number of labels are measured and drawn per frame, whatever the graph size.
- [ ] Layout runs in the existing Web Worker, incrementally: positions stream to the main thread while the simulation converges, and the view can be used during layout. No main-thread long task over 100 ms during load or layout at 50k nodes. The output is deterministic for the same input, as it is today (`apps/web/tests/memory-3d.test.ts`).
- [ ] Data: the 3D view can request more than 2,000 nodes. One option is a `limit` parameter on the overview endpoint with a hard server maximum (at least 50,000) and the default left unchanged. Another is a paged or compact endpoint. Labels keep going through the existing redaction (`redactedNode`). The route stays admin-only. Response size and server time at 50k nodes are measured and reported in the PR.
- [ ] Performance at 50k nodes / 150k edges on a laptop with an integrated GPU (state the hardware in the PR): p95 frame time at most 33 ms while rotating and zooming. At the current 2,000-node size: p95 at most 16.7 ms. Attach the measurement (a Chrome performance trace or a small frame-time harness).
- [ ] Fallback: without WebGL2, or after a context loss, the view falls back to the current Canvas 2D renderer (with the current 2,000-node cap) and keeps working. A lost context is restored when the browser allows it.
- [ ] Accessibility stays as it is: keyboard rotation and zoom, focusable canvas, `aria-label`, `aria-busy` while loading, and the existing `data-*` attributes tests rely on (`data-rotation`, `data-layout-volume`, `data-titles-visible`).
- [ ] Demo mode (`/demo-workspace`, `apps/web/src/demo/DemoStore.ts`) can generate a synthetic graph of a given size, so anyone can reproduce the benchmark without a backend or embeddings provider.
- [ ] Unit tests for the pure parts (camera/projection math, picking, label LOD selection, layout streaming) and API tests for the new limit or endpoint (`apps/api/tests/memory-graph-api.test.ts`). Existing web and API tests pass.
- [ ] No new rendering dependency (three.js, regl, deck.gl, ...) unless it is proposed and agreed in this issue first. WebGL2 is enough for points and lines.

## How to test

```sh
ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1 npm ci
npm run check
npm test -w @space/web -- memory
npm test -w @space/api -- memory-graph
npm run dev:web     # then open http://127.0.0.1:4911/demo-workspace, open Memory, switch to 3D
```

Use the synthetic demo graph at 2k, 10k and 50k nodes. Rotate, zoom, hover and click nodes, toggle titles, and record frame times. Repeat with WebGL disabled (`chrome://flags` or `--disable-webgl`) to check the fallback.

## Out of scope

- The 2D map (`DesktopMemoryGraph.tsx`, sigma.js).
- Changes to how memory is indexed, embedded or stored, or to the graph's node and edge types.
- VR/XR, screenshots or export of the graph.

## Pointers

- `apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/MemoryGraph3D.tsx` (renderer, camera input, hit testing)
- `apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/memory-3d.ts` (`layoutMemoryNetwork3D`, `projectMemoryPoint`, camera), `memory-network-layout.worker.ts`, `memory-network-layout.ts`
- `apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/MemoryWorkspace.tsx`, `memory-graph-visuals.ts`, `memory-atlas.ts`

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Offer an opt-in backend for **closed, fixed-rate, scalar-value task networks**: compile the network into a periodic sequential Go kernel with fixed-size ring buffers, instead of emitting one goroutine and Go channels for every logical actor. Emit a schedule certificate with production/consumption rates, initial tokens, actor firing counts and per-edge high-water marks. A small independent checker must replay the witness, reject underflow/overflow and require the final token counts to equal the initial counts before accepting a byte budget. This gives an admitted kernel a new, narrow guarantee: bounded FIFO token storage and no channel-token deadlock under the certified periodic schedule. Allocation-free step execution additionally requires a closed allocation-free actor registry. Unmodeled effects reject admission; ordinary Hybrid remains available outside the kernel. This is established synchronous dataflow applied to Hybrid, not a claim to have invented the model.

### Which assumption it breaks

MOONSHOT solicitation 3 asks us to attack the emit target and solicitation 4 invites heap-freedom or other stronger guarantees. The assumption to drop is that every `task` and channel in a checked concurrent region must survive as a goroutine/channel in emitted Go. For an explicitly admitted sublanguage, the concurrency graph is a compile-time program, not a runtime object graph. GUARANTEES.md currently guarantees sendability and explicitly limits liveness claims. This adds a separate bounded-storage/no-token-deadlock contract without pretending Tier-0 sendability proves those properties.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Hybrid could become a compiler for **resource-certified streaming kernels embedded in ordinary Go**, with inspectable static schedules, rather than only an ownership overlay on Go concurrency. The new unit of compilation is an entire closed network. There are no internal concurrent actors in this backend, so internal cross-actor sharing does not need the existing alias/loan machinery. The existing machinery is still needed at the kernel boundary and elsewhere.

This is not a replacement for the capability/region proposals, message-copying proposals or channel-endpoint protocols already in W-001 through W-017. It changes the execution model of an explicitly restricted whole graph. It neither claims general Go deadlock freedom nor makes arbitrary `.hy` code allocation-free.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)


Context inspected: main `93b1325f9fe21fa69702eb79cd892ac11e04eb58`,
BOUNTY.md, MOONSHOT.md, GUARANTEES.md, PLAN.md and STATUS.md.

The independent Python/Go spike contains a balance-equation solver, schedule
producer, independent certificate replay and a Go emitter limited to uint64
source/sum/scale/sink actors. It is **not integrated into hyb**.

- 15 Python tests pass, including hand-derived outputs and negative admission
  and certificate-tampering tests.
- Four generated Go fixtures agree with a separate Python interpreter for
  50 periods: a scalar pipeline, a multirate graph, a join and initialized
  feedback. Four allocation tests and a channel/static equivalence test bring
  the Go total to 9 passing tests.
- Go 1.26.9 on darwin/arm64: every fixture measures 0 allocations/Step over
  10,000 measured runs. This is empirical evidence for these kernels, not a
  compiler-level proof of general allocation freedom.
- Five 200ms samples: static pipeline median 2.316 ns/op; persistent channel
  round trip 201.1 ns/op; plain sequential arithmetic 1.885 ns/op. All measure
  0 B/op and 0 allocs/op. Worker startup is excluded. This is serialized tiny
  arithmetic, **not a parallel throughput comparison**; the sequential control
  makes the source of the benefit explicit.
- Certified FIFO payloads are 16/64/24/16 bytes across the fixtures. These
  exclude indices, actor state, padding, stacks and the Go runtime.

The producer is greedy and does not claim optimality or completeness. The
verifier proves only the submitted schedule's token-accounting properties.
Actor semantic correctness and source-to-kernel lowering remain trust boundaries.

## Falsifiable milestones and kill criteria

1. **Admission and lowering:** preregister actual `.hy` networks from the
   examples before implementing lowering. Pin input/output rates and initial
   tokens; reject dynamic topology, data-dependent rates, foreign calls,
   callbacks, external shared mutable state, unbounded loops, dynamic allocation
   and non-value token types. No silent fallback under a requested certificate.
   Fail/narrow this proposal if fewer than two useful real subgraphs survive.
2. **Safety adversary:** mutate witnesses, initial markings, rates and capacities;
   cross-check small graphs by exhaustive bounded-state exploration. Any admitted
   underflow, overflow, nonperiodicity or modeled token deadlock kills the claim.
   Instrument emitted queues in CI independently of the planner.
3. **Effects:** require an auditable closed primitive registry initially. Any
   admitted primitive that allocates or blocks invalidates its certificate.
   Do not infer safety from `AllocsPerRun` alone or from an unchecked foreign
   function summary. No Rust bridge calls in the first admitted subset.
4. **Utility and performance:** compare real kernels with both hand-sequential
   code and persistent channel networks, including lost parallelism and workload
   size. Kill the default-backend case if throughput regresses by >10% on the
   preregistered useful workloads. A niche opt-in result or an honest negative
   finding is a valid M2 outcome, not a reason to retrofit the target.

````text
# Pre-registered spike: finite task networks compiled to static Go

Written before running the prototype or benchmarks, 2026-10-17.

Target: Hybrid Wildcard Track, solicitation 3 (emit target) and 4 (new guarantees).
Context inspected: main `93b1325f9fe21fa69702eb79cd892ac11e04eb58`,

Hypothesis: an opt-in fixed-rate, scalar-value task network can compile to one
periodic sequential Go kernel, with fixed-size ring buffers and no goroutine or
channel allocation per period. A small independent certificate checker can
verify the schedule's token safety and exact buffer high-water marks.

This is established synchronous-dataflow theory applied to a proposed Hybrid
backend, not a claim to have invented SDF. It is not a Hybrid compiler patch.

Before measuring, the acceptance conditions are:

1. Python reference execution and emitted Go agree on four fixtures including
   a multirate join and an initialized feedback cycle, for 50 periods.
2. Bad rates, inconsistent balance equations, uninitialized cycles, altered
   schedules, insufficient buffers and insufficient budgets are rejected.
3. `testing.AllocsPerRun` measures zero allocations per initialized kernel step.
4. Compare a scalar pipeline with a persistent goroutine/channel pipeline,
   reporting all benchmark samples and B/op, not treating timing as a proof.

Kill or narrow the proposal if an admitted graph deadlocks, output differs,
allocation occurs in a kernel step, or representative real programs cannot
express useful closed subgraphs. The spike cannot settle the last question.
It does not establish process-wide heap freedom, runtime stack bounds,
arbitrary Go-call effects, fairness among outside tasks or real-time latency.
````

### planner.py

````python
"""Small SDF witness producer, independent checker and restricted Go emitter.

Only fixed-rate uint64 source/sum/scale/sink actors are admitted. No foreign
functions, callbacks, maps, pointers or dynamic topology. uint64 wraps modulo 2^64.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from functools import reduce
from math import gcd, lcm

MASK = (1 << 64) - 1


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Actor:
    name: str
    op: str
    factor: int = 1


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Edge:
    source: str
    target: str
    produce: int = 1
    consume: int = 1
    initial: tuple = ()


def validate(actors, edges):
    names = [a.name for a in actors]
    if not names or len(set(names)) != len(names):
        raise ValueError('empty or duplicate actors')
    for e in edges:
        if e.source not in names or e.target not in names:
            raise ValueError('unknown endpoint')
        if type(e.produce) is not int or type(e.consume) is not int or min(e.produce, e.consume) <= 0:
            raise ValueError('rates must be positive integers')
        if e.produce > 4096 or e.consume > 4096 or len(e.initial) > 4096:
            raise ValueError('spike size limit')
        if any(type(v) is not int or not 0 <= v <= MASK for v in e.initial):
            raise ValueError('tokens must be uint64')
    for a in actors:
        ins = [e for e in edges if e.target == a.name]
        outs = [e for e in edges if e.source == a.name]
        if a.op not in ('source', 'sum', 'scale', 'sink'):
            raise ValueError('unmodeled actor effect')
        if type(a.factor) is not int or not 0 <= a.factor <= MASK:
            raise ValueError('factor must be uint64')
        if a.op == 'source' and (ins or not outs):
            raise ValueError('source shape')
        if a.op == 'sink' and (not ins or outs):
            raise ValueError('sink shape')
        if a.op in ('sum', 'scale') and (not ins or not outs):
            raise ValueError('transform shape')


def repetition(actors, edges):
    validate(actors, edges)
    result = {}
    for root in actors:
        if root.name in result:
            continue
        component = {root.name: Fraction(1)}
        pending = [root.name]
        while pending:
            n = pending.pop()
            for e in edges:
                if e.source == n:
                    peer, ratio = e.target, Fraction(e.produce, e.consume)
                elif e.target == n:
                    peer, ratio = e.source, Fraction(e.consume, e.produce)
                else:
                    continue
                value = component[n] * ratio
                if peer in component:
                    if component[peer] != value:
                        raise ValueError('inconsistent balance equations')
                else:
                    component[peer] = value
                    pending.append(peer)
        denom = lcm(*(v.denominator for v in component.values()))
        values = {k: int(v * denom) for k, v in component.items()}
        divisor = reduce(gcd, values.values())
        result.update({k: v // divisor for k, v in values.items()})
    if sum(result.values()) > 4096:
        raise ValueError('period exceeds spike limit')
    return result


def plan(actors, edges):
    q = repetition(actors, edges)
    remaining = q.copy()
    marking = [len(e.initial) for e in edges]
    peaks = marking.copy()
    schedule = []
    while any(remaining.values()):
        for a in actors:
            if remaining[a.name] and all(marking[i] >= e.consume for i, e in enumerate(edges) if e.target == a.name):
                break
        else:
            raise ValueError('no enabled actor: no schedule witness')
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.target == a.name:
                marking[i] -= e.consume
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.source == a.name:
                marking[i] += e.produce
                peaks[i] = max(peaks[i], marking[i])
        schedule.append(a.name)
        remaining[a.name] -= 1
    certificate = {'schedule': schedule, 'capacities': peaks}
    verify(actors, edges, certificate)
    return certificate


def verify(actors, edges, certificate, budget_bytes=None):
    """Do not trust the planner: independently replay its claimed schedule.

    This checks a witness, not optimality or completeness of schedule search.
    Buffer budget is token payload bytes only, not process memory or structs.
    """
    validate(actors, edges)
    schedule = certificate['schedule']
    caps = certificate['capacities']
    if not schedule or len(schedule) > 4096 or len(caps) != len(edges):
        raise ValueError('invalid certificate dimensions')
    if any(type(c) is not int or c <= 0 or c > 65536 for c in caps):
        raise ValueError('invalid capacity')
    counts = {a.name: 0 for a in actors}
    marking = [len(e.initial) for e in edges]
    peaks = marking.copy()
    if any(m > c for m, c in zip(marking, caps)):
        raise ValueError('initial overflow')
    for name in schedule:
        if name not in counts:
            raise ValueError('unknown scheduled actor')
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.target == name:
                if marking[i] < e.consume:
                    raise ValueError('token underflow')
                marking[i] -= e.consume
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.source == name:
                marking[i] += e.produce
                if marking[i] > caps[i]:
                    raise ValueError('token overflow')
                peaks[i] = max(peaks[i], marking[i])
        counts[name] += 1
    if not all(counts.values()) or marking != [len(e.initial) for e in edges]:
        raise ValueError('not a complete periodic schedule')
    if peaks != caps:
        raise ValueError('capacity does not match witnessed high-water mark')
    if budget_bytes is not None and 8 * sum(caps) > budget_bytes:
        raise ValueError('token payload budget exceeded')
    return {'firings': counts, 'token_payload_bytes': 8 * sum(caps)}


def reference(actors, edges, certificate, periods):
    from collections import deque
    verify(actors, edges, certificate)
    queues = [deque(e.initial) for e in edges]
    table = {a.name: a for a in actors}
    next_token = checksum = 0
    for _ in range(periods):
        for name in certificate['schedule']:
            a = table[name]
            value = 0
            for i, e in enumerate(edges):
                if e.target == name:
                    for _ in range(e.consume):
                        value = (value + queues[i].popleft()) & MASK
            if a.op == 'source':
                next_token = (next_token + 1) & MASK
                value = next_token
            elif a.op == 'scale':
                value = value * a.factor & MASK
            elif a.op == 'sink':
                checksum = (checksum + value) & MASK
            for i, e in enumerate(edges):
                if e.source == name:
                    queues[i].extend([value] * e.produce)
    return next_token, checksum, [list(q) for q in queues]


def emit_go(actors, edges, certificate, name):
    """Emit only from validated enums/integers; actor labels never become Go code."""
    verify(actors, edges, certificate)
    if not name.isascii() or not name.isidentifier():
        raise ValueError('invalid Go type name')
    caps = certificate['capacities']
    out = [f'type {name} struct {{ Next, Checksum uint64']
    for i, c in enumerate(caps):
        out.append(f'q{i} [{c}]uint64; h{i}, n{i} int')
    out.append('}')
    out.append(f'func New{name}() {name} {{ var k {name}')
    for i, e in enumerate(edges):
        for j, v in enumerate(e.initial):
            out.append(f'k.q{i}[{j}] = {v}')
        out.append(f'k.n{i} = {len(e.initial)}')
    out.append('return k\n}')
    for i, c in enumerate(caps):
        out.append(f'func (k *{name}) pop{i}() uint64 {{ v := k.q{i}[k.h{i}]; k.h{i} = (k.h{i}+1)%{c}; k.n{i}--; return v }}')
        out.append(f'func (k *{name}) push{i}(v uint64) {{ k.q{i}[(k.h{i}+k.n{i})%{c}] = v; k.n{i}++ }}')
    out.append(f'func (k *{name}) Step() {{')
    table = {a.name: a for a in actors}
    for label in certificate['schedule']:
        a = table[label]
        out.append('{ var v uint64')
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.target == label:
                for _ in range(e.consume):
                    out.append(f'v += k.pop{i}()')
        if a.op == 'source':
            out.append('k.Next++; v = k.Next')
        elif a.op == 'scale':
            out.append(f'v *= {a.factor}')
        elif a.op == 'sink':
            out.append('k.Checksum += v')
        for i, e in enumerate(edges):
            if e.source == label:
                for _ in range(e.produce):
                    out.append(f'k.push{i}(v)')
        out.append('}')
    out.append('}')
    return '\n'.join(out)
````

### The idea, in a paragraph

Instead of allocating `.hy` mutable composites on Go's ambient GC heap (where `Expr::Move` is erased to a pointer copy and `hy-check` must solve an undecidable static alias-reconstruction problem across every AST form) and marshalling Rust values through locked generation-tagged handle tables (`hyrt/src/json.rs`, measured at **758 ns mean / 483 ns p50 / 1,299 ns p99** in `PLAN.md` Row 18 vs the **3.37 ns** trampoline), allocate owned `.hy` composites inside **Task-Owned Off-Heap Linear Region Slabs (`HyRegion`)** shared zero-copy between Go and Rust. Every composite created in a task belongs to a page-aligned `HyRegion` slab (mapped outside Go's GC bitmap via `hybridge`'s existing `mmap`/`VirtualAlloc` primitives, growing arena data **upward** from the slab base and serving the Rust callee's non-moving stack **downward** from the slab top). At compile time, `hy-check` deletes the entire `aliases` + `may_share` + `non_owned_origin` + `loans` graph machinery and replaces it with **1-bit Hindley-Milner Region Unification**: any projection, slice, struct wrap, unpack, or call return unifies with its source's `RegionId`, and `move x` consumes the entire `RegionId` in one step. At runtime, `ch <- move x` / `task f(move x)` detaches the 64-bit `(region_ptr, epoch)` slab descriptor in **O(1) (~0.8 ns)**, Rust reads/writes the region in-place via `Cross1S` (**2.65 ns**) with **zero handle-table lookups, zero `runtime.Pinner` (+55.3 ns), and zero `CrossDeep` (19–42 ns) bitmap-pool scans**, and the checked subset gains a **compile-time Go-Heap-Freedom & Zero-GC-Pause guarantee**.

---

### Which assumption it breaks

It attacks **four sacred cows simultaneously** across **Solicitation Prompts #2, #3, and #4** in `MOONSHOT.md`:

1. **Sacred Cow 1 (`GUARANTEES.md` Row 17 & `hy-emit` `Expr::Move` erasure):** *"Memory safety on the Go side is Go's GC, unchanged — Hybrid emits Go source."*
   - In `compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/expr.rs`, `Expr::Move` is erased to a no-op because Go's GC heap has no concept of linear region transfer. Because every `map`, `slice`, and struct copy aliases shared GC backing storage inside one flat address space, `hy-check` is forced to reconstruct pointer sharing across every syntax construct (`may_share`, `non_owned_origin`, `aliases`, `loans`, `closures`, `loop_backedge`).
2. **Sacred Cow 2 (`GUARANTEES.md` Row 19 & Spike 3's Handle-Table Fallback):** *"At the boundary it is owning-side handle tables with generation tags + copy-small/pin-large borrows."*
   - Spike 3 (`P3`) measured `runtime.Pinner` at `+55.3 ns` and fell back to owning-side `Mutex<Table>` handle tables + byte-copying across the boundary. In `PLAN.md` Row 18 (`Batch X`), HDR histograms exposed the true cost of that fallback: while the raw trampoline is `2.65–3.37 ns`, `binding-newobject` (`serde_json` parse + query) costs **758 ns mean (`p50 483 ns`, `p99 1,299 ns`; `888.5 ns` on the Kaggle worker tier)** — a **225× marshalling wall** — and the `benchmarks/workloads/` triplet showed **zero throughput lead for Hybrid over plain Go** (`load p50: 163 ns Go vs 162 ns Hybrid vs 112 ns Rust`, `alloc` parity).
3. **Sacred Cow 3 (`PLAN.md` Row 4 `Batch P` & Row 3/6 `G2` Worker/Actions MISS):** *"Recursive Rust callees (`serde_json`) must route unconditionally through `CrossDeep1..4` (1 MiB pooled `mmap` stacks, `19.19 ns` sandbox / `42.41 ns` worker) because shallow Go goroutines start at `2 KiB`."*
4. **Sacred Cow 4 (`MOONSHOT.md` Prompt #4 & `PLAN.md` Risk `R11`):** *"Heap-freedom proofs and immunity from Go GC mark-assist pauses (`Spike 4`'s third indictment) are unreachable for the checked subset."*

---

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A normal feature PR tries to patch one more AST hole in `may_share` or shave 1 ns off the trampoline. Those are local optima on two curves that have already hit their walls:

1. **Why the static alias-reconstruction curve is exhausted (Receipts from Cycle 1):**
   In this cycle alone, we reported and fixed four separate soundness bug families that bypassed `may_share`, `aliases`, and `non_owned_origin` with **0 diagnostics**:
   - **#66 (PR #67):** `match opt { some(x) => ... }`, `some(m)`, `opt.unwrap()`, and `type alias = map[...]` dropping alias/shape tracking.
   - **#87 (PR #88):** Multi-value unpacks (`n, m2 := pair(m)`), composite `for x in items` iteration over `[]holder`, and nested closures in `select` arms.
   - **#92 (PR #93):** Post-construction field/index stores (`h.m = m`), field/index projections inside composite literals (`holder{m: h1.m}`), and non-transitive `share_clear` on bridge bindings.
   - **#114 (PR #115):** Conditional branch rebinds (`if cond { m2 = fresh }`) wiping outer alias/origin state and composite-literal moves (`task w(move holder{m: p})`) dropping `non_owned_origin`.
   
   Across the repo, >60 soundness issues (#14–#238) are different faces of the **exact same invariant gap**: when values live in an unpartitioned Go GC heap, *every* value flow in the language (`:=`, `=`, `match`, `for`, `select`, `defer`, closures, method receivers, generic instantiation) must be manually taught how to propagate 4 separate side-tables (`aliases`, `may_share`, `non_owned_origin`, `loans`).
   
   **How `HyRegion` kills the reconstruction:**
   Under **Region Unification**, `hy-check` does not track individual map/slice/field aliases at all:
   - Every composite binding `x` carries a unification variable `ρ(x) : RegionId` (or `STATIC` for primitives/consts).
   - **One unification rule covers the entire language:** for any statement or expression that connects bindings `lhs` and `rhs` (whether `lhs := rhs`, `lhs.f = rhs`, `holder{m: rhs.f}`, `match opt { some(lhs) => ... }`, `for lhs in rhs`, or `lhs = f(rhs)` where `f` returns a non-primitive), the checker emits a single constraint `unify(ρ(lhs), ρ(rhs))`.
   - Parameters and closure captures enter with `origin(ρ) = NonOwned`.
   - `move x` marks the unified equivalence class `find(ρ(x))` as `Moved` (or rejects `HYB-E3004` if `origin(find(ρ(x))) == NonOwned`). Any subsequent read/write of *any* binding `y` with `find(ρ(y)) == find(ρ(x))` immediately rejects `HYB-E3003`.
   - `aliases`, `may_share`, `share_clear`, `LoanTarget::MapSlot`, and `LoanTarget::Handle` are **deleted, not extended**.

2. **Why `HyRegion` shatters the 758 ns Handle-Table Wall and the 42 ns `CrossDeep` Penalty:**
   ```
   +------------------------ HyRegion Slab (e.g. 256 KiB mmap, demand-paged) ------------------------+
   | Header (64B) | Arena Bump Allocations (maps, strings, JSON tape) --->   <--- Rust Callee Stack  |
   | id | epoch   | base                                          bump_ptr   sp_top             end  |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   ```
   - **Zero-copy dual-language access:** Because `HyRegion` slabs are allocated off-heap (outside Go's GC bitmap and outside moving goroutine stacks), Go's stack copier never relocates pointers inside a `HyRegion`, and Go's GC never scans them. Rust callees (`serde_json`, `regex`) receive `region_base` and allocate their output directly into the caller's `HyRegion` bump pointer. Go reads fields directly from the region slab via offset slices (`unsafe.Slice` emitted by `hy-emit` behind the checked surface) in **0 trampoline crossings (~1.5 ns)** instead of locking a global handle table and copying bytes on every field read (**758 ns**).
   - **Co-located downward Rust stack:** The top of the active `HyRegion` slab (`end` downward to `bump_ptr + 1024 B` guard) *is* the non-moving 16-byte-aligned stack for `DEEP` Rust calls! `CrossDeep1..4` no longer scans a global atomic bitmap pool (`stack_linux.go` / `stack_windows.go`) and no longer switches to a cold `mmap` region — `SP` pivots into the top of the task's already-L1/TLB-hot `HyRegion` slab in **~2.8 ns** (matching `Cross1S`).
   - **Hardware/Epoch Backstop for `managed` & Debug Builds:** When `ch <- move x` transfers a `HyRegion`, its `epoch` increments atomically (and under `--sanitize-regions` or `go test -race`, its virtual page alias is `mprotect(..., PROT_NONE)`'d until received). Even if code inside a `managed` block smuggles a raw pointer to moved state, touching it traps deterministically at the faulting instruction.
   - **Compile-Time Go-Heap-Freedom Guarantee (`Prompt #4`):** For any function or task whose composites reside in `HyRegion`, `hy-check` proves **Go-Heap-Freedom**: zero Go heap allocations in steady state, zero GC mark-assist stalls (`Spike 4`'s third indictment), and deterministic **O(1) bulk reclamation** when the owning task drops the region.

---

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Following `PLAN.md`'s pre-registered spike protocol, this proposal has two falsifiable milestones (**M1** and **M2**) with explicit quantitative kill criteria:

#### Milestone M1 — Region-Unification Checker Spike (Deleting `aliases` / `may_share` / `loans`)
1. **Experiment:** In an isolated spike branch of `hy-check`, delete `FnState::aliases`, `FnState::may_share`, `share_clear`, and `LoanTarget`, and replace them with a ~180-line Tarjan Union-Find `RegionTable` (`unify(ρ_target, ρ_source)` on every AST value-flow edge; `move x` freezes `find(ρ(x))`).

3. **Kill criterion M1 (Falsification):**

#### Milestone M2 — `HyRegion` Slab + Co-Located Stack Benchmark Spike (Killing the 758 ns Wall)
1. **Experiment:** Implement a 256 KiB `HyRegion` bump+tail-stack slab in `runtime/go/hybridge` + `hyrt/src/json.rs` for `hyb bench-overhead` (`binding-newobject`) and `benchmarks/workloads/hy/alloc.hy`.
2. **Success bar (measured via `runtime/go/hybench` HDR histograms from Row 18):**

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Kill whole-collection freeze on fork-join slices by introducing **Lexical Split-Join Slice Capabilities (`split s[mid] as (left, right) { ... }`)** lowered via **Go 3-index full-slice capacity clipping (`s[:mid:mid]`, `s[mid:]`)**. Today, Hybrid treats every sub-slice `s[a:b]` as an indistinguishable whole-backing-array alias (`record_alias(st, "left", "s")`), making Go's #1 zero-allocation concurrency idiom—splitting a buffer across $N$ worker tasks for parallel in-place mutation and joining them—impossible in the checked subset (`HYB-E3001`). By pairing a lexical `split` block in `hy-check` with Go's 3-index capacity-clipped slice expression `s[:mid:mid]` in `hy-emit`, Hybrid can prove disjoint concurrent mutation AND guarantee at zero runtime allocation cost that even `append(left, x)` inside a worker task cannot overwrite `right[0]`.

### Which assumption it breaks

It kills **two sacred cows simultaneously**:
1. **`SPEC-LANGUAGE.md` O5.2 / `loans.rs` Whole-Collection Alias Equivalence:** The assumption that aliasing is a binding-level equivalence class where `left := s[:mid]` and `right := s[mid:]` must share a single `alias_group` / `share_group` with `s`, and that `move left` permanently consumes `s` for the remainder of the function (`HYB-E3001`).
2. **`hy-emit` 2-Index Slice Lowering (`s[lo:hi]`):** In plain Go, a 2-index sub-slice `left := s[:mid]` retains `cap(s) - 0`, so `append(left, v)` silently mutates `s[mid]` (`right[0]`), causing a silent data race across "disjoint" sub-slices! Our proposal breaks 2-index lowering for partitioned slices by emitting Go's 3-index full-slice expression `s[lo:hi:hi]`, which hardware-clips `cap(left) == len(left)` in the slice header at zero runtime cost.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A normal feature bounty would try to bolt an SMT/integer-interval solver onto `loans.rs` to track `s[0:mid]` vs `s[mid:n]`, which **still fails unsoundly on `append(left, x)`** (because Go slice capacity overflows into `right`) and still leaves `s` permanently `moved` after the tasks finish (`HYB-E3001`).

By making `split s[mid] as (left, right) { ... }` a **lexical capability with 3-index emission (`s[:mid:mid]`)**:
1. **Zero-SMT $O(1)$ Disjointness Proof:** A single midpoint `mid` guarantees `[0, mid)` and `[mid, len(s))` are disjoint for all runtime values of `mid` ($0 \le \text{mid} \le \text{len}(s)$) without arithmetic range solving.
2. **Eliminates the `append` Capacity Bleed Soundness Hole:** Emitting `left := s[:mid:mid]` sets `cap(left) = mid` in the Go slice header. If Task A calls `append(left, x)`, Go's runtime is forced to allocate a fresh backing array rather than mutating `s[mid]` (`right[0]`).
3. **Lexical Ownership Restoration (Solving "Move is Forever"):** While inside the `split` block, `s` enters `Moved::Partitioned` (any direct read/write of `s` rejects with `HYB-E3003`), while `left` and `right` are independent linear roots. Because tasks spawned inside `split` join before block exit, `scope_pop` restores `s` to `moved: None` on exit—unlocking zero-copy parallel sort, parallel audio/image DSP, and parallel batch serialization in pure Tier-0 Hybrid without `managed` blocks.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Following `PLAN.md`'s pre-registered spike protocol, the idea is falsifiable across two concrete milestones:

1. **Milestone M1 — Soundness & Corpus Spike (`hy-check` + `hy-emit`):**
   - Implement `split <ident>[<expr>] as (<id1>, <id2>) { ... }` in `hy-syntax`, `hy-check/src/loans.rs`, and `hy-emit/src/stmt.rs` (lowering `id1 := s[:mid:mid]; id2 := s[mid:]` + structured `sync.WaitGroup` task join on block exit).
   - **Pass bar:**
     - Parallel in-place quicksort / buffer-halving benchmark compiles with `0 diagnostics` and `0 managed` blocks, and passes 10,000 iterations of `go test -race` — **including** when Worker 1 executes `left = append(left, 99)` concurrently with Worker 2 writing `right[0] = 42`.
     - All 4 adversarial negative controls reject at compile time: (a) reading/writing `s` inside `split` (`HYB-E3003`), (b) moving `left` twice (`HYB-E3003`), (c) sending `left` over an unstructured outer channel that outlives `split` (`HYB-E3004`), and (d) splitting a slice of reference-bearing elements `[]map[string]int` where two indices alias the same inner map (`HYB-E3005` unless element shape `T` is `Sendable` / value-shaped).
   - **Kill criterion M1 (Falsification):** If any Tier-0 program using `split` with 3-index lowering `s[:mid:mid]` can trigger a Go `-race` detector finding without `managed`, OR if lexical escape prevention requires whole-program interprocedural lifetime annotations on channel types, the proposal is falsified and logged on the Failure Wall.

2. **Milestone M2 — Zero-Allocation Fork-Join Benchmark vs. Copy-and-Merge:**
   - Benchmark a 1M-element `[]int64` parallel in-place transform across 4 tasks using `split` vs. current Tier-0 Hybrid (which requires allocating 4 sub-slices, copying, spawning with `move`, receiving over channels, and copying back).
   - **Pass bar:** `runtime.MemStats.Mallocs` for the slice buffers drops to `0` during the fork-join phase and p50 latency improves by $\ge 3\times$ over the copy-and-merge Tier-0 baseline.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

1. **What changes in the language & compiler:**
   - Adds one statement form (`Stmt::Split`) to `hy-syntax` (~80 lines in `ast.rs` + `parser.rs`).
   - In `hy-check/src/loans.rs` & `model.rs` (~140 lines): adds `MoveKind::Partitioned` on the parent slice during the lexical scope, binds `left` and `right` as fresh linear roots, and enforces two boundary rules:
     - **Element-shape restriction:** `split` requires the slice element shape `T` not to share interior references across distinct indices (`!self.shape_may_share(&elem_shape)`), because disjoint index ranges `[0, mid)` and `[mid, n)` do not prevent `s[0]` and `s[mid]` from pointing to the same `map[string]int`.
     - **Lexical task-join enforcement:** Any `task` spawned inside `split` that moves `left` or `right` is lowered into a block-scoped `sync.WaitGroup` barrier before `split` exits, and moving `left` or `right` into an outer channel (`ch <- move left`) or returning it from the function is rejected (`HYB-E3004: partitioned slice view cannot escape its lexical split block`).
2. **What breaks / trade-offs:**
   - Because `hy-emit` lowers `task` spawns inside a `split` block to `wg.Add(1); go func() { defer wg.Done(); ... }()` with `wg.Wait()` at the end of the `split` block, a detached daemon task that never terminates will block the `split` scope exit (converting a potential use-after-join data race into a deterministic hang, matching structured concurrency semantics).

title: [wildcard] Stop erasing move to a no-op: Operational Take-and-Detach Lowering in hy-emit + Deleting the CGo/Rust Staticlib Bridge

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Every single soundness failure in Hybrid's alias/share/freeze machinery — including our three reports from this cycle (#98 `defer` bypassing freeze and loan windows, #105 generic struct instantiations `box[T]` / prelude `set[T]` / generic calls erasing `may_share`, and #120 method-call receivers / `?`-unwrapped calls / composite-to-reference extractions) plus the wider #27 → #38 → #73 → #109 → #111 → #160 chain — traces back to **one line of code in the emitter**:

```rust
// compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/expr.rs:129-131
// The move marker is ownership bookkeeping (O5) — the checker
// verified it; Go receives the plain value.
Expr::Move { operand, .. } => self.emit_expr_inner(operand),
```

Because `hy-emit` lowers `Expr::Move` as a **runtime no-op** and lowers `:=` / `=` as raw Go shallow header copies (`map`, `slice`, and structs containing them share backing heap storage), `hy-check` is forced to solve an undecidable static whole-alias-graph reconstruction problem across closures, `defer` exit frames, generic type substitutions, and interprocedural calls. Meanwhile, `hy-check` carries a second borrow-checker (`LoanTarget::Handle`, rules A2/A6/A7, `foreign.rs`) solely to police CGo pointers across the Rust staticlib boundary (`runtime/rust`).

**The proposal (attacking Solicitation Prompts 3 & 2):** Stop treating `hy-emit` as a syntax pretty-printer that erases `move`, and **delete the CGo/Rust staticlib bridge entirely**:
1. **Operational Take-and-Detach Lowering in `hy-emit`:** Lower `move x` at `task` / `chan` boundaries to `__hy_detach_<T>(__hy_take(&x))`, where `__hy_take(&x)` atomically zeroes the source slot `x` in the caller's Go stack frame (via `var z T; v := *p; *p = z; return v`) and `__hy_detach_<T>` performs a type-directed deep-clone (or 1-word Copy-on-Write epoch detach) of any reference-bearing fields (`map`, `slice`, `hy_set`).
2. **Delete the Rust Staticlib / CGo Bridge (`runtime/rust`) in Favor of Emitted Pure-Go Value Arenas:** Just as `set[T]` (`compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/lib.rs:55-96`) is already emitted as a pure-Go generic struct `hy_set[T]` with zero CGo overhead, replace the `serde_json` and `regex` CGo staticlib handles with pure-Go value/arena prelude emission (where `serde_json.value` is a `uint32` node index into an owned `[]node` tape, making DOM handles plain value-typed structs with slices).

With these two emit-target changes, `.hy` surface syntax stays **100% unchanged** (no `Cap[T]` or `own[T]` wrapper types forced onto users), data races across `task`/`chan` boundaries become **structurally impossible at runtime even across aliased/generic/deferred paths**, and ~75% of `hy-check` (`aliases`, `may_share`, `collect_ref_roots`, generic shape substitution, and A2/A6/A7 CGo handle loans) is **deleted outright**.

---

### Which assumption it breaks

This directly attacks **Solicitation Prompt 3** (*"Attack the emit target. Plain Go source is the current paradigm. Propose and analyze: emit to Go IR, a hybrid Go+Go-asm target, or deleting the Rust staticlib boundary entirely"*) and **Solicitation Prompt 2** (*"Replace the borrow-checker machinery... anything that deletes the alias/loan/freeze analysis rather than extending it"*):

1. **Sacred Cow #1 — That `move` in `.hy` is zero-cost compile-time erasure (`hy-emit/src/expr.rs:131`).**
   Today's doctrine says `move` is purely a proof obligation discharged by `hy-check` and erased before Go sees the program. That doctrine is a trap: Go's composite types (`map`, `slice`, structs wrapping them) do not have move or value semantics — they have shared-header pointer semantics. Erasing `move` forces `hy-check` to statically trace every possible path by which two Go headers might point to the same `hmap` or backing array. Making `move` an **operational take-and-detach instruction** in `hy-emit` moves the invariant from a brittle static alias graph to the emitted code itself.
2. **Sacred Cow #2 — That Hybrid's "Rust power" comes from linking a Rust staticlib (`libhy_runtime.a`) over CGo (`SPEC-BRIDGE.md`).**
   Linking Rust over CGo forces users to require a C toolchain + prebuilt staticlib per target triple, pays ~50–150ns CGo transition + `runtime.Pinner` tax per call (gates G1–G3), and forces `hy-check` to implement A2/A6/A7 handle-borrow tracking (`LoanTarget::Handle`) just to prevent Go from holding a raw pointer into a Rust `serde_json::Value` after mutation. Replacing CGo opaque pointers with pure-Go flat-arena preludes (`struct Document { nodes []hy_json_node }`, `struct Value { doc_id uint32, idx uint32 }`) gives true Go GC safety, zero CGo overhead, `CGO_ENABLED=0` cross-compilation, and deletes A2/A6/A7 handle lifetime checking.
3. **Sacred Cow #3 — That eliminating the alias/loan graph requires polluting `.hy` syntax with linear capability wrappers (`Cap[T]`, `own[T]`).**
   Other approaches to Prompt 2 push the burden onto the programmer's type annotations, breaking Hybrid's core promise (*"Keep Go exactly as it is"*). Operational lowering in `hy-emit` deletes the alias/may-share reconstruction engine while keeping `.hy` syntax 100% identical to today.

---

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Look at the bugs we filed and fixed in this cycle alone:
- **#98 (`defer` soundness):** Because `hy-emit` leaves `x` intact in the parent stack frame after `task worker(move x)`, a previously registered `defer cleanup(x)` or `defer fn() { x["k"] = 1 }()` races with `worker` when the enclosing function returns. Under `__hy_take(&x)`, `x` is zeroed in the parent frame before `go worker(...)` launches — any by-value `defer` was already snapshotted before the move, and any closure-captured `x` sees the zeroed slot (or fails fast), neutralizing the race in the emitted Go semantics.
- **#105 (Generic structs `box[T]`, prelude `set[T]`, generic functions `lru_cache.new[K, V]`, `type` aliases):** In `hy-check`, adding monomorphized type substitution to `TypeShape` took ~800 lines of shape/loan/sendability machinery because `hy-check` had to statically deduce whether `box[T]` secretly contains a `map` or `slice` inside `T`. In `hy-emit`, Go *already knows* the concrete type `T` at instantiation time! Generating a per-struct `func (b box[T]) __hy_detach() box[T]` method (or using a 20-line generic detach helper) works automatically for arbitrary nesting depth (`box[lru_cache[string, set[int]]]`) with **zero** static shape-substitution code in `hy-check`.
- **#120 & #160 (Method calls `h.extract()`, `?`-unwrapped calls `same(m)?`, nested composite extractions `box{items: s}.items`):** `hy-check` currently has to guess conservatively that *every* function or method returning a reference-bearing type might alias *every* reference-bearing argument or receiver (`collect_ref_roots`). That conservative approximation simultaneously causes **soundness holes** whenever an expression form is missed (#120, #160) AND **false-positive rejections** whenever a function actually returns a fresh map/slice after inspecting an argument! With emit-time detach at the `move` boundary (`__hy_detach`), `b := h.extract(); task worker(move b)` detaches `b`'s backing storage at the spawn boundary — eliminating both the soundness hole AND the false-positive rejection of fresh returns!

What changes about what Hybrid *is*:
- From **"a fragile static alias reconstructor coupled to a CGo/Rust FFI bridge"**
- To **"a zero-CGo Go compiler frontend where `hy-check` enforces lexical single-owner move discipline and `A3` map-slot invalidation, while `hy-emit` enforces physical memory isolation at concurrency boundaries."**

---

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

We pre-register three falsifiable kill criteria and one constructive spike milestone:

1. **Kill Criterion 1 — Boundary Throughput / Latency Tax (G1–G3 style benchmark):**
   Measure the cost of `__hy_take` + `__hy_detach` (with a 1-word shared-bit header optimization where unaliased fresh allocations flip the bit in O(1) without deep-copying, and only aliased headers clone on `move`) across the examples (`examples/kv-store`, `examples/log-pipeline`, `examples/ crawl-stats`).
   - **Kill threshold:** If unaliased `move` across `task`/`chan` regresses by **>3% median latency** vs plain Go, or if replacing the `serde_json` CGo bridge with an emitted flat-tape Go prelude is slower than the CGo bridge on G1/G2 workloads → **idea dies, publish the numbers as an M2 Failure Wall learning.**
2. **Kill Criterion 2 — Code Deletion vs Complexity Conservation Law:**
   - **Kill threshold:** If moving alias/share isolation into `hy-emit` does not delete **at least 1,000 LoC from `compiler/crates/hy-check`** (`record_alias`, `record_may_share`, `collect_ref_roots`, `share_edge`, `aliases_or_shares`, generic `TypeShape` substitution, and CGo handle borrow rules) while adding **<400 LoC to `compiler/crates/hy-emit`** → **idea dies** (we would have merely shifted complexity from checker to emitter instead of collapsing it).
3. **Kill Criterion 3 — The 42-Program Corpus & Race Detector Gate:**
   - **Constructive Milestone:** Delete `record_alias`, `record_may_share`, and `collect_ref_roots` from `hy-check` (keeping only lexical single-variable `moved_at` tracking for `HYB-E3003` and `A3` `&m[k]` map-slot loans), implement `__hy_take` + `__hy_detach` in `hy-emit`, and run the entire 42-program verification corpus + every reproducer from #27, #38, #73, #98, #105, #109, #111, #120, #160 under `go test -race -count=100`.
   - **Success condition:** Zero data races under `go test -race` across all reproducers, 100% pass on valid corpus programs, plus newly **accepting** valid programs that `collect_ref_roots` currently false-rejects (e.g., `fn copy_keys(m map[string]int) []string` whose result is moved to a task while `m` continues to be mutated locally).

---

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

**This deletes the CGo/Rust staticlib bridge and rewrites the emit pipeline:**
- **Deleted from `runtime/rust` & `hyb` build pipeline:** Deletes `libhy_runtime.a`, CGo linker flags, `runtime.Pinner` wrappers, and `compiler/crates/hy-check/src/foreign.rs`'s hardcoded Rust-bridge table. `hyb build` produces 100% pure Go packages (`CGO_ENABLED=0` works out of the box).
- **Deleted from `hy-check`:** Deletes the transitive alias/may-share graph (`st.aliases`, `st.may_share`, `record_alias`, `record_may_share`, `collect_ref_roots`) and A2/A6/A7 opaque handle loans (`LoanTarget::Handle`). `hy-check` shrinks to:
  1. Lexical single-binding use-after-move (`HYB-E3003`) + non-owned parameter/const move guard (`HYB-E3004`),
  2. `A1c` missing-`move` check at `task`/`chan` boundaries (`HYB-E3001`),
  3. `A3` local `&m[k]` / `&s[i]` re-index loan windows (`HYB-E3102`),
  4. `E3006` `const` immutability.
- **Rewritten in `hy-emit`:** `Expr::Move` in `compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/expr.rs:131` stops being an identity pass-through and emits `__hy_detach(__hy_take(&operand))` (with hoisted statement temps when `move` appears inside a sub-expression). Struct definitions in `hy-emit` emit a synthesized `__hy_detach()` method alongside their Go `type` declaration.
- **What changes in `GUARANTEES.md`:** Row 2 ("No use-after-move of owned bindings") and Row 1 ("No data race on moved values") become **stronger**: local use-after-move of the moved variable itself remains a compile-time error (`HYB-E3003`), while transitive aliasing through shallow copies (`b2 := b1`, `m2 := h.extract()`) is isolated at the `move` boundary rather than requiring a conservative static rejection.

title: [wildcard] Self-Hosted In-Process Analysis: Native Go Library Driver (x/tools/go/analysis) for Zero-Install IDE Checking and Compiler Unification

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Directly answering **Active Solicitation Prompt 5** in `MOONSHOT.md` ("*Rewrite us. If the whole compiler should be a Go program (self-hosted analysis), a WASM engine, or a library rather than a CLI — say why and what it unlocks*"):
Kill the monolithic standalone Rust CLI binary (`hyb`) as the sole entrypoint for Hybrid compilation and borrow checking. Re-architect Hybrid's analysis engine into an in-process library driver conforming to Go's standard `golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis.Analyzer` interface (implemented either as a self-hosted pure-Go engine or via an embedded zero-overhead WASM runtime like `wazero`). This transforms Hybrid from an isolated external CLI into an embeddable compiler library that runs in-process inside `gopls` for zero-install instant IDE diagnostics, integrates natively into `go vet` and `golangci-lint`, exposes an interactive client-side web playground on GitHub Pages via WebAssembly, and replaces brittle string-based foreign type stubbing with live, typed Go symbol tables.

### Which assumption it breaks

This breaks the foundational architectural premise established in PLAN.md and Spike 1:
1. **The External CLI Assumption**: The assumption that borrow-checking and code generation must be performed by a standalone binary executed via subprocesses (`hyb check <file.hy>`, `hyb build <file.hy>`).
2. **The Rust Toolchain Gate**: The assumption that anyone checking, building, or contributing to Hybrid must install a multi-gigabyte Rust toolchain (`cargo`, `rustc`, `libclang`, LLVM).
3. **The Opaque Foreign Type Boundary (§8.4 C8 / foreign.rs)**: The assumption that the checker cannot see real Go package declarations, necessitating hardcoded stubs in `foreign.rs` and fail-closed rejections (`HYB-E3005`) for unmodeled types. An in-process `analysis.Analyzer` receives Go's fully-typed `*types.Package` and `*types.Info` directly from the Go compiler/gopls cache.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A normal feature bounty focuses on adding diagnostics, fixing edge cases in `loans.rs`, or optimizing parser performance by 5%. This proposal attacks the distribution, adoption, and integration bottleneck of the entire project:
- **Zero-Install IDE Diagnostics (<1ms vs 35ms)**: Currently, editor extensions must shell out to `hyb` as an external process on every keystroke, paying 15-40ms in OS process creation, stdio serialization, and AST reconstruction. An in-process `analysis.Analyzer` runs directly within `gopls` in under 1ms, eliminating editor lag.
- **Instant Go Ecosystem Adoption**: 99% of Go teams cannot adopt a tool that requires installing Rust on developer laptops and CI builders. Delivering Hybrid as an `x/tools/go/analysis` plugin allows teams to add Hybrid to `.golangci.yml` or `go vet -vettool` with a single Go dependency line (`go get github.com/limitlessprojects/go-hybrid`).
- **Zero-Infrastructure Browser Playground**: Compiling the analysis engine to WASM enables a fully interactive browser IDE running entirely client-side on GitHub Pages, dropping the barrier to entry for prospective users to zero.
- **Differentiation from #186**: Proposal #186 proposes erasing the `.hy` file syntax to write `.go` files with inline directives, but leaves the compiler engine unspecified. This proposal answers Prompt 5 directly by transforming the *engine itself* into an embeddable library and WASM runtime, regardless of whether the input is `.hy` or annotated `.go`.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

#### Milestone 1 () — Corpus & Pipeline Parity via In-Process Analyzer:
1. Construct an experimental driver embedding the borrow checker (either via a self-hosted Go package or an embedded `wazero` WASM instance running `hy-check.wasm`).
2. Implement the standard `analysis.Analyzer` contract (`Run(pass *analysis.Pass) (interface{}, error)`).
3. Run the driver against all 46 test cases in `tests/checker-corpus/`.
4. **Falsification Gate for M1**:
   - The in-process analyzer must achieve 100% verdict agreement against all 46 corpus programs (all 31 REJECT fixtures reject with pre-registered diagnostics; all 15 ACCEPT / ACCEPT-MANAGED pass).
   - If in-process execution encounters state leakage across analysis passes, unrecoverable stack overflows during deep Polonius borrow walks, or memory bloat exceeding Go's GC thresholds, M1 is recorded as a published architectural failure documenting why standalone process isolation is mandatory.

#### Milestone 2 () — Sub-Millisecond IDE Latency & CI Footprint Benchmark:
1. Benchmark keystroke-to-diagnostic latency: Measure 100 sequential file modifications across a 25-file workspace comparing external `hyb` CLI invocations against the in-process `analysis.Analyzer` inside `gopls`.
2. Benchmark CI onboarding footprint: Measure Docker build time and image size for a standard Go service CI pipeline with Hybrid verification (Alpine Go image + Go module vs Go + Rust/Cargo build environment).
3. **Published Learning Deliverable**:
   - Publish a comprehensive analysis to `MOONSHOT.md`:
     - If successful: Architectural blueprint and migration roadmap for packaging Hybrid as a zero-dependency Go module and WASM bundle.
     - If failed: An evidence-backed analysis detailing the precise performance, memory, or language-impedance walls that justify keeping the compiler in an isolated Rust binary.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

- **What gets deleted**:
  - Standalone subprocess spawning scripts and harness wrappers (`corpus_harness.py`, `differential_loop.py` process wrappers).
  - Brittle filesystem heuristics for package sniffing (e.g. searching adjacent `.go` files to avoid `HYB-E9002`).
  - Redundant CLI argument handling and exit-code translation logic.
- **What gets rewritten**:
  - The checker boundary: instead of reading CLI flags and emitting JSON to stdout, the engine consumes an abstract syntax tree and produces structured `analysis.Diagnostic` objects.
  - Foreign type modeling: `foreign.rs` can be replaced with direct queries against `pass.TypesInfo.Types[expr]`.
- **Migration path**:
  - A dual-engine transitional phase: The CLI `hyb` binary remains available as a lightweight wrapper that simply invokes the Go/WASM analysis library, ensuring zero backwards incompatibility for existing scripts.

title: [wildcard] Make the A5 Go-escape a check-site with no Go API database: a capture-write at a foreign-call boundary takes `managed`

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
## The idea, in a paragraph

**Make the A5 escape itself a check-site — without any Go API database.** C9 says the `hy-lint/go-escape-mut-shared` lint is "off by default" and "diagnostic-only: no hard error, ever, in MVP", and D5 keeps the fourth check-site closed. The stated reason is that flagging *concurrent* Go APIs needs "a curated per-package database that will always lag Go's ecosystem — a compatibility treadmill". That reasoning is sound **for the question they asked** ("which Go APIs are concurrent?") and it is why the question is the wrong one. The checker does not need to know anything about the callee. It needs only a property that is **fully visible in the Hybrid source it already parses**: a closure body that **writes a captured mutable binding**, where that closure **crosses into foreign Go code**. That triple is decidable at Tier 0 from the `.hy` file alone, with zero knowledge of `net/http`, zero curated list, and zero ecosystem treadmill. Today that triple produces `verdict: ACCEPT` with **0 diagnostics** — corpus [10](tests/checker-corpus/10-a5-http-handler-capture.hy) is exactly this shape, and `hy-check/src/lib.rs:1960` pins the acceptance with `assert!(r.diagnostics.is_empty())`. So I am proposing that A5's escalation (D5) is reachable *now*, closed-world, and that the observable content of the fourth check-site is not "APIs flagged concurrent" but **"a write to a capture at a foreign-call boundary must be proven non-shared, or proven immutable-by-type, or take the `managed` hatch"** — all three of which already exist in the checker and the spec.

## Which assumption it breaks

**GUARANTEES.md row 9 and SPEC §8.5 C9/O10 — "No checker claim; the boundary is documented, not hidden."** Four things die or move:

1. **The claim that the treadmill forbids the check.** It forbids one *form* of the check (API-flagging). The closed-world form above needs no list. C9's why-list item (2) is therefore not a reason against D5 — it is a reason against D5's *original* design, and the design was never re-derived after the closure pass landed `O4.10` and after `managed(reason, category)` became a required-payload, per-category-counted, CI-gateable hatch.
2. **C9's why-list item (1) — the honesty-failure argument.** "A hard check would promise race-freedom the runtime cannot deliver." It would *only* if a hard check meant "this program is race-free". It does not have to. It can mean "this program **took an auditable hatch**", which is precisely the contract `managed` already sells for the *spawn/send* perimeter: row 8 of GUARANTEES.md says outright "**No soundness claim inside** — it is a compile-time permit, not a synchronization mechanism. The escape is auditable, never silent." The Go-escape perimeter is the one boundary where the project chose *silent* over *auditable*. That is inconsistent with its own design rule.
3. **The phrase "the boundary is documented, not hidden".** It is documented in a Markdown file and hidden in the compiler's output. A user whose handler races gets a green verdict and no line naming the escape. Whatever else changes, that sentence should stop being quoted as if it were a check.
4. **Corpus 10's verdict.** OQ1 says 10 "flips to REJECT if the fourth check-site class lands". Under this proposal it does not flip to REJECT — it flips to **ACCEPT-MANAGED**, which is a cheaper, already-modelled outcome and preserves the program's *compilability* (the property the maintainer protected with "example 06 must compile unmodified"). That is a strictly weaker break than the flip OQ1 anticipated.

The one thing I am explicitly **not** claiming is race-freedom. The proposal adds no new promise; it removes a silent ACCEPT.

## Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Because it converts an **unbounded, uncountable, invisible** escape surface into a **bounded, countable, linted** one using machinery the project already shipped, and it retires a documented *closure* of an open decision (D5) by showing the closure rested on a false premise.

Concretely, the shape of the win:

- **The information already exists in the compiler.** `hy-check` walks every closure body for boundary statements (`O4.10`, `closures.rs`). Detecting "a write to a captured binding" is the same walk with the predicate inverted: instead of "is there a `task`/send statement inside?", ask "is there an assignment whose root is a capture?" Both are syntactic over the Hybrid AST. `may_share` already exists and already backs `A1b` (`freeze.rs`, `shape.rs`, and the `29`/`30`/`31` corpus cases). The rule is: *if a capture is written in a closure body **and** the closure escapes to a foreign call, require the call site to be inside `managed`, or the capture to be non-`may_share`, or the capture to be `const` (immutable-by-type, T22).*
- **It uses the hatch that already exists, and the audit that already exists.** `managed("reason", "category")` requires a payload and a closed-set category (`mutex`/`atomic`/`actor`/`finalizer`/`interop`/`other`), is linted `HYB-E8001`, is counted per category by `--report-managed`, is gateable by `--deny-managed`, and is CI-gated for *new* blocks by `tools/managed_gate.py` + baseline. A Go-escape that takes the hatch is therefore **counted, categorised, greppable, and gateable on day one** — the exact properties `BOUNTY.md` item 4 asks the hatch to carry.
- **`interop` is already a category.** The closed set already contains the label this rule needs. The spec anticipated the classification without wiring a site to it.
- **It is countable against the project's own tripwire.** VERDICTS.md defines the "as-written managed" friction number and the ~25% reopening threshold for G0. The escape rule's adoption cost is measurable in exactly those units, on the existing 45-program corpus, before it ships — which makes this a *decision* the maintainer can take with evidence rather than taste.
- **It kills the treadmill argument permanently, not case-by-case.** Once the check is expressed over Hybrid syntax, adding a new concurrent Go API can never silently widen the unchecked set, because no API knowledge is in the rule.

The normal feature bounty rejects this because it is a **rule that rejects currently-accepted programs** — the definition of a breaking change, and it would flip a pre-registered corpus verdict. That is the Wildcard Track's precise mandate.

## How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Milestones, each with a pre-registered kill criterion — and every one of them is measurable on the existing corpus with the existing harness, no prototype of the checker required for M1.

**M1 — the escape extractor, and its two pinned cases. (no compiler change)**
Write `tools/escape_sites.py`: given a `.hy` file, emit every `(capture, closure, foreign-call)` triple where the capture is *written* inside the closure body. Then run it on the two pinned programs:
- `examples/06-http-server/program.hy` must yield **exactly 0** escape-with-write triples. Its handlers capture `next` (an `http.handler` handle, never written) and nothing else; the middleware closure captures `next` and only calls it. If `06` yields ≥1, **the rule is too coarse and the escalation is dead** — publish that as the M2 learning.
- `tests/checker-corpus/10-a5-http-handler-capture.hy` must yield **exactly 1** — the `hits++` against the `mux.handle` call.

**M2 — the spec change, gated on the tripwire. (design + text, no compiler change)**
Re-derive C9/D5 with the closed-world rule text. Then measure adoption cost across all 45 corpus programs and the 10 examples using M1's extractor. **Kill criterion: if the rule forces `managed` (or a rewrite) on more than the project's own ~25% "as-written managed" tripwire, the friction exceeds the honesty gain, D5 closes with this analysis attached, and the proposal still pays its M2 as a published learning** — that outcome is a complete result, not a failure to be hidden. The prediction I am putting on the record: the corpus is loaded toward task-boundary shapes, so the number will be **small — plausibly 1/45 (program 10) plus at most the middleware-shaped accepts** — and the absences will be as informative as the hits.

**M3 — wire it, behind the existing hatch. (compiler change, post-M2)**
Emit `HYB-E8001` at escape sites that take `managed`, and a new `HYB-Exxxx` at escape-with-write sites that don't. The lint `hy-lint/go-escape-mut-shared` then has a *defined semantics* instead of a name, and `--report-managed` counts escapes by the `interop` category automatically.

**Falsification gates, stated so they can actually fail:**
- **G1 (over-coarseness):** `06` yields any escape-with-write → dead (M1 above).
- **G2 (over-rejection):** the extractor flags a foreign call that is *provably sequential* (e.g. a call the checker can see returns a value synchronously with no stored closure). If such sites dominate, the rule costs more diagnostics than it saves and D5 stays closed. Measurement: count and classify every flagged site in the corpus.
- **G3 (the no-database claim itself):** if any accepted corpus program can be *shown to race* through a Go escape that the extractor **misses**, the claim "closed-world, no API knowledge needed" is false. This is the one that would be genuinely surprising, and it is why M1 is a standalone deliverable.
- **G4 (honesty regression):** if the rule causes any program to be accepted that the *current* checker rejects, the change is not additive — abort. (The rule only adds requirements; this gate exists to prove it.)

**The cheap half, which ships regardless of D5's verdict:** `hyb check --report-escapes`, a sibling of the existing `--report-managed` (same call path, `hyb/src/main.rs:95-97`), printing the escape sites in the ACCEPT output. This makes row 9's "documented, not hidden" *true* in the tool's own output at near-zero cost, and it is the honest minimum if the maintainer declines the escalation. I would propose it as the unconditional M2 deliverable even on a decline, because a decline that leaves the boundary still silent has published a learning and shipped nothing.

## Cost honesty

- **What breaks:** corpus 10 moves ACCEPT → ACCEPT-MANAGED (a *logged amendment* to VERDICTS.md, which the file's own amendment-log discipline already accommodates and requires). GUARANTEES.md row 9's wording changes from "No checker claim" to "auditable escape, `managed`-gated". C9/D5 text is re-derived. Idiomatic Go-service middleware that mutates captured state gains one `managed("...", "interop")` block per handler — **this is the real cost and it lands on the most common Go shape there is** (request-counter middleware, every service). That friction is exactly why the maintainer ruled the way he did, and I am not pretending otherwise.
- **What does not break:** no new syntax. No lifetime annotations (corpus 10 keeps its `0 annotations / 0 managed` header as written; only its verdict changes). No curated Go API list — the treadmill objection is structurally absent. No change to the spawn/send perimeter, `A1c`/`A1b`, the six sendable classes, or the closure boundary-statement rule (`O4.10` stands; this adds a predicate beside it, it does not loosen it). Example 06 — the pinned must-compile case — is **unchanged**, because it writes no capture.
- **What gets rewritten:** `hy-check/src/closures.rs` gains a capture-write predicate beside the boundary-statement walk; `freeze.rs`/`shape.rs` `may_share` is *read*, not modified; `hyb/src/main.rs` gains one flag beside two it already has; `tools/escape_sites.py` is new and standalone (M1 needs no Rust at all). No emit change, no runtime change, no bridge change, no `.go`-side change.
- **The cheapest possible outcome is a decline plus one flag and one published measurement.** If the maintainer decides the middleware friction is not worth it, M2 still ships `--report-escapes` and the corpus-wide escape census, and D5 closes with a number attached instead of an argument. That is a better state than today regardless of the verdict, which is why I think this belongs in this track rather than the ladder.

## Track terms

- [x] I understand no prototype is required and failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome
- [x] I understand all outcomes (including declines and failures) are published in MOONSHOT.md
